details.readme:
# Claude Code Plugins Directory

A curated directory of high-quality plugins for Claude Code.

> **⚠️ Important:** Make sure you trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it. Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software are included in plugins and cannot verify that they will work as intended or that they won't change. See each plugin's homepage for more information.

## Structure

- **`/plugins`** - Internal plugins developed and maintained by Anthropic
- **`/external_plugins`** - Third-party plugins from partners and the community

## Installation

Plugins can be installed directly from this marketplace via Claude Code's plugin system.

To install, run `/plugin install {plugin-name}@claude-plugins-official`

or browse for the plugin in `/plugin > Discover`

## Contributing

### Internal Plugins

Internal plugins are developed by Anthropic team members. See `/plugins/example-plugin` for a reference implementation.

### External Plugins

Third-party partners can submit plugins for inclusion in the marketplace. External plugins must meet quality and security standards for approval. To submit a new plugin, use the [plugin directory submission form](https://clau.de/plugin-directory-submission).

## Plugin Structure

Each plugin follows a standard structure:

```
plugin-name/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json      # Plugin metadata (required)
├── .mcp.json            # MCP server configuration (optional)
├── commands/            # Slash commands (optional)
├── agents/              # Agent definitions (optional)
├── skills/              # Skill definitions (optional)
└── README.md            # Documentation
```

## Plugin names are immutable

The `name` field in a marketplace entry is an **immutable slug**. Once a plugin has been published, its `name` must not change — users have it installed under that slug, and renaming it breaks their install with a `plugin-not-found` error.

- To change how a plugin is labeled in the UI, set or update `displayName` instead.
- If a rename is genuinely unavoidable, add an entry to the top-level `renames` map in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` so existing installs auto-migrate:

```json
"renames": {
  "old-name": "new-name"
}
```

The Claude Code plugin loader reads this map and transparently rewrites the old slug to the new one on the user's next sync.

## Skill-bundle plugins

When a plugin's source repository ships skills (`SKILL.md` files) without a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, the marketplace entry can declare the skills directly using `strict: false` and an explicit `skills` array.

```json
{
  "name": "example-bundle",
  "description": "Brief description of the bundled skills.",
  "author": { "name": "Author Name" },
  "category": "development",
  "source": {
    "source": "git-subdir",
    "url": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk.git",
    "path": "packages/agent-skills",
    "ref": "main",
    "sha": "<commit sha>"
  },
  "strict": false,
  "skills": [
    "./skill-a",
    "./skill-b",
    "./skill-c"
  ],
  "homepage": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk"
}
```

Each path in `skills` is relative to `source.path` and points at a directory containing a `SKILL.md`. Paths can reach deeper than a single level — for example, `["./libA/skill-1", "./libB/skill-2"]` exposes a curated subset across multiple library subdirectories. Each skill is registered as `<plugin-name>:<skill-name>` in Claude Code.

For the underlying schema, see [Strict mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces) in the marketplace documentation.

## License

Please see each linked plugin for the relevant LICENSE file.

## Documentation

For more information on developing Claude Code plugins, see the [official documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins).

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/installation.md) for provider configuration and manual MCP registration. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.19), 24.x (>=24.11), or 26+, plus npm. # Dub Anything

Dub films and shows into another language **in each actor's own voice**, with
the original music and sound effects intact. It runs on your own PC, and an AI
coding agent directs the dub line by line, the way a dubbing director would.

You give it a video file. You get the same file back as
`my-show (dubbed).mkv`: the dub plays by default, the original audio is one
track away, and subtitles in both languages are included.

It dubs Japanese, Spanish, Korean and Chinese into English, and English into
Japanese, Spanish and Cantonese (yue). Need another language? Just ask: your agent adds the new
pair as part of the job. Once it works, please
[send it back](#other-languages-and-hardware) so everyone gets it.

## Demos

| A Japanese anime, dubbed into English | A Japanese film, dubbed into English |
|---|---|
| [![A Japanese anime, dubbed into English](https://img.youtube.com/vi/qXosYS-cTXk/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qXosYS-cTXk) | [![A Japanese film, dubbed into English](https://img.youtube.com/vi/2DsFAoTbQ8E/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2DsFAoTbQ8E) |

## What makes it different

Most dubbing tools run a fixed pipeline: transcribe, translate, clone each
speaker from one clip, speed up whatever runs long. Dub Anything differs where
a listener notices:

- **An agent directs, line by line.** It works out who says each line from
  voice matching, video frames and the dialogue, fixes what speech recognition
  misheard, writes a translation timed to the actor, and triages every QA flag.
  It tells you which lines are guesses instead of hiding them.
- **Each line is acted like the original.** The cloned voice is prompted with
  the actor's own delivery of that very line, so a shout stays a shout and a
  murmur stays a murmur.
- **Each line takes the actor's time.** Every take is re-timed to end where the
  actor stops, so turns land where they did in the original, without dead air.
  Each line's length is predicted before rendering, so the translation is
  written to fill the time.
- **Every line is checked.** Each rendered line is transcribed back. A garbled
  one gets fresh takes, up to three rounds, and the best take is kept.
- **It reads the picture.** Burned-in captions become the transcript (and often
  name the speaker), and text on screen, like title cards and signs, can be
  translated as subtitles placed beside it.
- **The rest stays original.** Between lines you hear the original soundtrack,
  so songs, laughs and names stay the actor's own.
- **Chosen by ear.** The defaults were picked by listening to the alternatives
  side by side. What was measured is in [docs/research.md](docs/research.md).

## What you need

- **macOS (Apple Silicon M1/M2/M3/M4 or Intel)** with Metal (MPS) acceleration,
  or **a Windows PC with an NVIDIA GPU** with at least 6 GB of memory. A 16 GB
  card runs everything at once. (Linux should be a short port; see
  [below](#other-languages-and-hardware).)
- **Disk space:** about 40 GB for VoiceStudio, the models and the tools'
  environments, plus room to work: a movie in both voices used about
  85 GB until it was cleaned up.
- **An AI coding agent** that reads [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): Claude Code,
  Codex, Cursor or similar.
- **[VoiceStudio](https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio)**, the open-source
  voice engine Dub Anything drives. The setup guide installs it.

## Getting started

1. **Set up once** with [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md): VoiceStudio, its
   models, ffmpeg and uv.
2. **Open this folder in your agent** and ask, for example:

   > Dub D:\movies\my-show.mkv into English.

3. **Pick a voice** when it asks ([below](#choosing-a-voice)). Into Japanese
   or Spanish there's nothing to pick.
4. **Let it work.** The machines separate, transcribe, render and check while
   the agent directs each part as soon as it's drafted. It tells you if
   something needs you.
5. **Listen.** At the end you get the dubbed file and a short list of moments
   to check, with their times. Tell the agent what to change, and it
   re-renders just those parts.

The agent can't hear, so you're the ears: you judge the acting, the voices and
the mix, and you decide what may be cloned or shared.

The steps above are the normal direct workflow. Jellyfin is an optional way to
queue library videos with a headless director; its separate setup is in
[docs/jellyfin.md](docs/jellyfin.md). Direct dubs do not need the plugin, worker,
or updater. The [script guide](scripts/README.md) identifies each entry point.

## Choosing a voice

| | **Actor's voice** (default) | **American** |
|---|---|---|
| Sounds like | The actor speaking English, with their own accent | Native American English, converted toward each actor's voice |
| Best for | Live action | Anime and animation |
| Trade-offs | Accented English | Less like the actors in live action, a little less of the acting, and a few times slower to render |

Not sure? Ask for both. Each gets its own audio track, and you switch between
them in your player (the actor's voice plays by default). The American voice
has so far been used on Japanese sources.

Into Japanese or Spanish, the actor's voice is the only one: each actor speaks
the new language with their own accent.

## How long it takes

A short clip takes minutes. A movie in both voices takes about seven
hours of machine time on a laptop RTX 4090, nearly all of it on the GPU; the
actor's voice alone takes about half that. The agent directs while the renders
run, and on a long video it can split the directing across helper agents.

## Privacy

Your video and audio stay on your machine: the models run locally, and the
internet is only used to download them. Your agent does read the transcripts
and the video frames it looks at, so those go wherever your agent's model runs.

## Responsible use

Only dub media you have the rights to, and only clone voices with the consent
the use requires. A dub made from someone else's film or voice is for private
use unless you have permission.

## How it works

1. **Split** the video into ~3-minute parts at pauses in speech.
2. **Separate** the voices from the music and effects (Mel-Band Roformer).
3. **Transcribe** each part with Whisper large-v3, with two other recognisers
   as a second opinion, and burned-in captions where there are any.
4. **Cast** each line by matching voices across the whole show, checked
   against video frames.
5. **Direct** (the agent): correct the transcript, translate, and time every
   line to the actor.
6. **Voice** each line. The actor's voice: OmniVoice clones the actor, prompted
   with their own delivery of that line. American: IndexTTS speaks native
   English following the actor's delivery, and Chatterbox converts it to the
   actor's voice.
7. **Fit, mix and check.** Each take is re-timed to end where the actor stops,
   mixed over the original background, and transcribed back to catch garbled
   words.
8. **Deliver** into your video file. Nothing is re-encoded, and every stream is
   checked against the original before the file is replaced.

<summary>The whole pipeline in one diagram</summary>

![How a dub gets made](docs/process.png)

The diagram is [docs/process.jg](docs/process.jg), a
[Jumpgate](https://github.com/swax/jumpgate) file. It is rendered with
`npm run render -- <path>/docs/process.jg --width 1800 --height 2700` from
Jumpgate's `packages/jumpgate`.

</details>

## Documentation

- [docs/jellyfin.md](docs/jellyfin.md): Jellyfin dashboard plugin, local queue,
  and headless Codex or Claude Code directors
- [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md): installing everything, step by step
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): the agent's instructions, and a dub from start to
  finish
- [docs/directing.md](docs/directing.md): the directing workflow, every tool,
  and the gotchas
- [docs/languages/](docs/languages/README.md): notes for each language, and
  how to add one
- [docs/research.md](docs/research.md): what was measured and tried
- [docs/roadmap.md](docs/roadmap.md): what's next

## Running it without an agent

The scripts are plain Python, so you can drive a dub yourself and write the
directed scripts by hand. With VoiceStudio's Python
(`$py = "C:\git\VoiceStudio\.venv\Scripts\python.exe"`),
`scripts/dub_anything.py` runs the machine work of a whole dub:

```powershell
& $py scripts\dub_anything.py new D:\movies\my-show.mkv --voices both   # a job named my_show
& $py scripts\dub_anything.py run my_show --watch   # prep, then render each part marked ready
# write work\my_show-NN\script.json for each part, then:
& $py scripts\dub_anything.py ready my_show 01
& $py scripts\dub_anything.py status my_show
```

<details>
<summary>Or one step at a time</summary>

With the backend running (`scripts/backend.py start`):

```powershell
& $py scripts\split.py videos\episode.mkv                      # long video -> parts at pauses
& $py scripts\dub.py prep videos\episode-parts\episode-01.mp4  # upload, separate, transcribe
& $py scripts\draft.py episode-01                              # careful transcript, suggested cast
# write work\episode-01\script.json and the cast in work\voices.json
& $py scripts\dub.py generate episode-01 --match-level         # clone, time, mix, export
& $py scripts\lineqa.py episode-01                             # check each rendered line
& $py scripts\assemble.py episode --parts 1-4                  # one video with both audio tracks
& $py scripts\deliver.py D:\movies\episode.mkv actor=videos\episode-parts\dubbed\episode.dubbed.mp4
```

Some steps need their own environments (`separate.py`, `subs.py`,
`second.py`; see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md)).

</details>

The workflow, the script format and every tool are in
[docs/directing.md](docs/directing.md).

## Other languages and hardware

Ask for a language pair that isn't here yet, and your agent adds it as part of
the job. The voices aren't the limit: VoiceStudio clones voices in hundreds of
languages. What's new for each language is what the scripts know about it: the
phrases Whisper hallucinates in it, the recognisers that give second opinions,
and how QA compares a take with its line. That lives in one module,
`scripts/languages/<code>.py`. The agent writes it, then checks the pair on a
short test dub before adding it, as
[docs/languages/](docs/languages/README.md#adding-a-language) describes.

**Please send new languages back.** If your agent added a language or a pair,
open a pull request with its module, its notes (`docs/languages/<code>.md`)
and the pair's entry in `PAIRS`, so the next person gets it ready-made.

The models run on Metal MPS (on Apple Silicon macOS) or CUDA (on Windows/Linux)
and fall back to the CPU without it, slower. Video is encoded with
Apple VideoToolbox on macOS, NVENC on Windows/Linux when NVIDIA is present,
else x264. Platform differences (paths, desktop app runtime detection, GPU locks,
audio separation environments) are handled automatically across macOS and Windows.

## Contributing

Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome, new languages most of all.
[docs/directing.md](docs/directing.md) explains how the pieces fit. Python is
formatted and linted with ruff (`uvx ruff format`, `uvx ruff check`), and
[docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md) shows how to turn on the pre-commit check.

`videos/` and `work/` are git-ignored so that source media, transcripts and
voice references stay out of the repository. Don't force-add them, and use
invented examples in docs and commit messages.

## Built on

Dub Anything is direction and glue around excellent open-source work:

- [VoiceStudio](https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio): the voice backend

  American voice

Website · Download · What changed · Screenshots · Parity status · Documentation

# Horizon A Rust rewrite of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 built for one-to-one vanilla parity, checked against the game itself with differential tests. Every subsystem matches vanilla in all 281 parity harnesses, on Linux and macOS: 100% of what the harnesses compare (see [Project status](#project-status)). The native client is playable on Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows. > Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. ## What changed in v2026.10.13.1 The latest release ([notes](https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon/releases/tag/v2026.10.13.1)): - **Horizon's own menus:** a new title screen, world list, options and pause menu in the launcher's style, over a live frozen landscape. The vanilla look is still available: Options → Interface → Menu style → Classic. - **Graphics settings, Simple and Advanced:** presets (Performance, Balanced, Quality, Ultra), or every rendering, quality, display and performance setting, each with a short description and its cost, plus a performance overlay. - **Much faster rendering:** for example, at render distance 8 over a village, 363 → 2,409 FPS on an RTX 4080. Render distance 32 still stutters in places. - **Fixed:** no sound on Linux; Linux builds that only ran on the machine they were built on; a missing DLL on Windows (the launcher no longer needs the Visual C++ runtime); memory growing and the frame rate dropping near villages (mobs were duplicated when chunks reloaded); resource preparation failing on Linux with "Missing … java-objc-bridge" ([#41](https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon/issues/41)); the hand and held item at high FOV; missing swing animations. ## Download Horizon is downloaded only through **the Horizon launcher**: get it from [playhorizon.dev](https://playhorizon.dev) or from [the launcher's releases](https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon/releases?q=launcher-v&expanded=true) (the newest `launcher-v*` release, currently [launcher-v0.1.3](https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon/releases/tag/launcher-v0.1.3)), for Linux x86-64, macOS Apple Silicon or Windows x64. The launcher installs and updates the game, prepares its resources from your own copy of Minecraft, starts the client or a dedicated server, and updates itself. **You need** Minecraft: Java Edition installed with the official launcher, with 26.3 played once; Python 3.10 or newer and Java 25 (a JDK, e.g. Eclipse Temurin 25) for the one-time resource preparation; and a GPU with Vulkan on Linux and Windows, or any Apple Silicon Mac. ### The launcher
It lists Horizon's releases and installs the build for your platform, shows each release's patch notes, updates Horizon and itself, and doubles as a command-line tool and an MCP server. See [the launcher's README](launcher/README.md). ## Screenshots Captured in the Rust client itself, with vanilla assets and no mods or shaders. ### Menus and settings
The vanilla menus are one setting away: Options → Interface → Menu style → Classic. See [Graphics settings](docs/graphics.md). ### In game
Vanilla world generation ported to Rust (terrain, aquifers, carvers, features, villages and the Nether), every block model with smooth lighting and biome tints, the vanilla sky and fog, mobs, the HUD, chat and advancements: everything in these frames is drawn by Horizon.
## What it does Horizon reimplements the Minecraft Java client and its game logic in Rust, one subsystem at a time, and compares each piece with the vanilla game. Each `tools/test_*_parity.py` harness drives the same inputs through Horizon and through the vanilla client and server bytecode from your own copy of the game, then checks that the outputs are identical. It is for players and developers interested in game reimplementation, and for anyone who wants to see how far a behaviour-exact native rewrite can go. The [native client](docs/native-client.md) opens on a vanilla-style title screen with world creation and selection, and generates worlds with the Rust port of the vanilla generators: noise terrain, aquifers, surface rules, carvers and placed features, all checked against vanilla. It streams and lights chunks on worker threads and renders every vanilla block model with smooth lighting, biome tints, the vanilla sky, sun, moon, stars and clouds. Gameplay includes: - validated player physics, health and hunger; - mining with vanilla tool rules and loot tables; - placing, crafting, chests and furnaces; - dropped items, particles and sounds; - passive and hostile mobs with combat and vanilla AI, including guardians, shulkers, illagers, ravagers, the wither, the ender dragon fight, the breeze, the creaking, the sniffer, the happy ghast, llamas and the copper golem; - villagers that take jobs, trade, restock, meet at the bell and sleep in beds, on a port of vanilla's brain; - raids and pillager patrols; - dispensers, crafters, the loom and the recipe book; - every command, scoreboards and teams, the player list, subtitles and the HUD overlays; - boats, minecarts, item frames, paintings and armor stands; - shields, maps, books, fireworks, beacons, advancements and statistics; - Anvil saves, joining vanilla servers, and opening a world to LAN. ## Agent control AI agents and scripts can play Horizon. `horizon-ctl`, shipped beside the game in every release folder, is a command line that reads the game as JSON and acts like a player; `horizon-ctl mcp` serves the same commands as an MCP server (one tool per command, screenshots returned as images). ```sh horizon-ctl launch --world Survival --seed 5 --wait # finds the version the launcher installed horizon-ctl state # position, health, food, target, screen... horizon-ctl find-block birch_log # the nearest logs horizon-ctl goto -0.5 65 -2.5 --near 2.5 # walks there along a path horizon-ctl break -1 65 -3 # mines it; replies with the drops horizon-ctl open-inventory && horizon-ctl click-slot 0 # menus: slots, buttons by label, text fields ``` Commands block until the action is done and reply with what happened; errors are JSON with distinct exit codes, `horizon-ctl help` lists every command and `horizon-ctl COMMAND --help` explains one with examples. It talks to the game over a Unix socket on Linux and macOS and over a token-protected localhost port on Windows. See [Agent control in the native client guide](docs/native-client.md#agent-control-horizon-ctl-and-mcp). ## Build from source For developers. Requirements: Rust 1.90 or newer, Python 3.10 or newer, JDK 25, and on Linux the ALSA and udev development headers (`libasound2-dev libudev-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu). Development and the vanilla harnesses run on Linux. Horizon contains no game files and never downloads them. It builds its resources from **your own copy** of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, verified against the checksums in `research-lock.json`: 1. **Client:** install Java Edition with the official launcher and play 26.3 once. Horizon reads `versions/26.3/`, `libraries/` and `assets/` from the launcher's game directory (`~/.minecraft` on Linux). If yours lives elsewhere, pass `--minecraft-dir` or set `HORIZON_MINECRAFT_DIR`. 2. **Server jar:** the 26.3 server jar, from the `downloads.server.url` in your launcher's `versions/26.3/26.3.json` (or [minecraft.net/download/server](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/download/server) while 26.3 is the current release). Pass it with `--server-jar` or set `HORIZON_SERVER_JAR`. It is only needed the first time. ```sh git clone https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon.git cd horizon cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar # needs JDK 25 cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- sounds # optional: sounds from your launcher install cargo run --release -p horizon-client ``` Everything prepared lands in the gitignored `.local/`. It is derived from the game: never commit it or share it. The client starts on the title screen. --- yovoice is an open-source, local-first audio and music creation studio for macOS and Windows. Turn text into expressive speech, natural cloned voices, complete vocal songs, and multi-track scores right on your machine. Featuring zero-shot voice cloning, emotional performance controls, AI music generation with lyrics, and General MIDI score arranging—**all running 100% locally with zero cloud API calls, zero per-character fees, and zero Python environment headaches.** ![yovoice creation workspace — browser preview](docs/images/yovoice-workspace.png) --- ## Why yovoice? - 🔒 **100% Local Privacy**: Runs entirely on your local GPU/CPU. Your manuscripts, reference voices, and creations never leave your computer. - 💸 **Zero Recurring Fees**: Say goodbye to per-character/per-minute meters and expensive cloud voice/music subscriptions. - ⚡ **Native C++ Performance (No Python Hell)**: Powered by [audio.cpp](https://github.com/0xShug0/audio.cpp) v0.9.1. Ships with bundled Windows CUDA 12.4/13.3 runtimes and native macOS Metal support. Double-click and create—no Conda or PyTorch conflicts. - 🎛️ **Creator Workstation**: Multi-take versioning for side-by-side comparison, waveform trimming, timeline scrolling, and clean stems/MIDI export. - 🤖 **MCP & AI Agent Ecosystem**: Connect DeepSeek, Qwen, Claude, OpenAI, or local Ollama to write scores and lyrics in seconds. Includes a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Cursor and Claude Code. --- ## Features - **Voice and expression** — use a reference voice, match a reference performance, adjust emotions, or describe the delivery in words. - **A complete audio workflow** — import or record reference audio, trim clips, preview speech, and export your work. - **Voice design and cloning** — VoxCPM2 offers text-guided voice design, controllable cloning, and transcript-assisted cloning with automatic multilingual handling, and 48 kHz output. - **Music generation** — describe a style, write lyrics with section markers, and generate full songs or instrumentals with ACE-Step 1.5; every take is kept as a version to compare. - **Score** — write each part by bar and beat, import MIDI or let an Agent write the score, then render it with a General MIDI sound font and a role-based mix; results are exactly repeatable and export to MIDI and stems. Windows updates download only the app (`-update.exe`) and keep the installed runtime; when a release recommends a newer runtime you can upgrade it in Settings → Inference engine. ![Install yovoice on macOS](docs/images/yovoice-macos-install.png) --- ## Quick Start 1. **Set up a model.** Download a model in Settings (e.g. Kokoro-82M for fast narration, or VoxCPM2 for cloning). 2. **Create a project.** Choose Story dubbing, Speech generation, Music, or Score. 3. **Add content.** Enter text, lyrics, or notes, then pick a character and adjust style. 4. **Generate audio.** Select Generate, then preview, compare takes, edit, and export. --- ## CLI & Agent Skill Give your agent the [yovoice Skill](https://github.com/leemysw/yovoice/tree/main/skills/yovoice) link and ask it to install the Skill and set up the local CLI, engine, and model: > Install this Skill and set up yovoice for local speech generation: https://github.com/leemysw/yovoice/tree/main/skills/yovoice Then describe what you want: > Read narration.txt using voice.wav as the reference voice, with a calm delivery, and save it as narration.wav. The agent runs the standalone CLI without opening the desktop app. See the [CLI guide](docs/cli.md) for details. --- Run `yovoice serve` to provide an authenticated HTTP API and MCP inference service for other machines. See the [API / MCP deployment guide](docs/api.md) for deployment and client examples. ## Development ```sh make install make app-run ``` See the [development guide](docs/development.md) for prerequisites. It also covers browser preview, tests, and project structure. --- ## Contributing Bug reports, feature suggestions, and pull requests are welcome. Include your platform, model, and steps to reproduce when reporting a problem. Run `make check` before submitting code changes. --- ## Acknowledgements - [audio.cpp](https://github.com/0xShug0/audio.cpp) by ShugoAI — the local audio inference engine. - [VoxCPM](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM) — voice design and cloning models, licensed under Apache-2.0. - [IndexTTS](https://github.com/index-tts/index-tts) — the speech synthesis models behind yovoice. - [OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) — voice design and cloning models. - [Qwen3-TTS](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS) — voice cloning, built-in voices, and text-guided voice design. - [ACE-Step](https://github.com/ace-step/ACE-Step-1.5) — music generation from style prompts and lyrics. - [go-meltysynth](https://github.com/sinshu/go-meltysynth), [MuseScore General](https://musescore.org/en/handbook/3/soundfonts-and-sfz-files#gm_soundfonts), [GeneralUser GS](https://www.schristiancollins.com/generaluser) and SGM-V2.01 by David Shan — the SoundFont synthesizer and sound fonts behind score rendering. - Kokoro — lightweight speech synthesis with built-in voices: [Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) and [Kokoro-82M-v1.1-zh](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M-v1.1-zh). --- ## Star History --- ## License [Apache-2.0](LICENSE). # Yarn Spinner for Godot (GDScript)

> [!CAUTION]
> This is Yarn Spinner for Godot (GDScript) Early Access 3.2. There will be bugs, we might change the API or features with an update, or something may break. We do not recommend you use this to ship a game just yet. 

Yarn Spinner for Godot (GDScript) is a pure-GDScript implementation of the Yarn Spinner dialogue system for the Godot engine. It runs compiled Yarn programs and aims for full feature parity with Yarn Spinner for Unity 3.2, including node groups, saliency, detours, smart variables, localisation, and voice over support.

Requires Godot 4.6 or later (not the .NET/Mono version).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Yarn Spinner for Godot (GDScript) is not yet for sale (it will always be available here for free, too). We rely on your support to keep everything free and accessible. If you want to support us during Early Access, you can support us on [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/YarnSpinnerTool) or [Patreon](https://patreon.com/secretlab). GitHub sponsors of $25 and above, and Patreon members of the "Scribe" or above tier will receive a license to the paid version when it is released.

Visit the [documentation](https://docs.yarnspinner.dev/yarn-spinner-for-godot/godot-gdscript) and [Yarn Spinner site](https://yarnspinner.dev) for more information.

> [!TIP]
> **Please submit issues or feature requests via this form during Early Access:** http://yarnspinner.dev/pre-release-feedback

## Samples

The samples live in their own project in the [YarnSpinner-Godot-Samples](https://github.com/YarnSpinnerTool/YarnSpinner-Godot-Samples) repository. 

The samples project ships without this addon: copy this repository's `addons/yarn_spinner/` folder into the samples project's `addons/` directory first (the samples README has step-by-step instructions), then open the project in Godot 4.6+, open the scene for the sample you want, and run it with "Run Current Scene" (F6).

The intention is that Yarn Spinner for Godot (C#) and Godot (GDScript) will ship with a full suite of samples on par with the samples supplied as part of Yarn Spinner for Unity.

## Differences from Yarn Spinner for Godot (C#)

Yarn Spinner for Godot (C#) is a port of Yarn Spinner for Unity that uses the core Yarn Spinner C# library directly. 

It requires the .NET-enabled build of Godot, a `.csproj`/`.sln`, and compiles Yarn scripts inside the editor via a C# import plugin. 

This GDScript version is a complete reimplementation of the Yarn Spinner runtime in pure GDScript, with no .NET dependency, no DLLs, no C# project needed. It works with the standard (non-.NET) Godot editor and export templates, making it accessible to GDScript-only projects. 

Yarn scripts are compiled with the Yarn Spinner compiler bundled with the addon (with `ysc` as a fallback), and both versions produce identical runtime behaviour from the same `.yarn` source files.

## Differences from Yarn Spinner for Unity

The VM, protobuf parser, library, and markup system were all written to match Unity's behaviour, and the runtime is checked against Yarn Spinner's own test plans, but there are some differences:

- **CLDR plural rules** -- `[plural]` and `[ordinal]` use the same CLDR plural rules as Yarn Spinner, for every locale it supports.
- **Culture** -- Unity formats the results of `string()`, `number()`, `bool()` and `format()` using the player's current culture. This implementation always uses the invariant culture, so `string(3.5)` is `3.5` on every device.
- **Extra built-in functions** -- As well as Yarn Spinner's built-in functions, this implementation provides `abs`, `clamp`, `lerp`, `inverse_lerp`, `smoothstep`, `pow`, `sqrt`, `sign`, `wrap`, `mod`, `length`, `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `first_letter_caps`, `plural` and `ordinal`. Unity doesn't have these, so scripts that call them won't run there unless you register matching functions.
- **Async model** -- Unity uses C# `async`/`await` with `YarnTask` and `CancellationTokenSource` chains. This implementation uses Godot signals and `await` with a simpler `YarnCancellationToken`. The behaviour is largely the same, but the presenter API signatures are different (signals instead of tasks).
- **Command discovery** -- Unity uses `[YarnCommand]` and `[YarnFunction]` attributes on methods. This implementation uses a naming convention (`_yarn_command_<name>` and `_yarn_function_<name>`), registering methods from `class_name` scripts when the dialogue runner starts, and from the rest of the scene tree once the scene is ready. When you export your game, the plugin records which scripts declare these methods, so the exported game doesn't need to search for them.
- **Error handling** -- Unity throws exceptions for invalid states (missing variables, bad option indices, etc.). This implementation reports them with `push_error`, and stops the dialogue when it can't safely continue.
- **Markup rendering** -- The built-in line presenter renders `[b]`, `[i]`, `[u]`, `[s]`, `[code]`, `[style]` and palette markers as BBCode. In Unity these are rendered by TextMesh Pro.
- **Execution limits** -- The virtual machine can optionally stop runaway scripts with `max_instructions_per_step` and `max_call_stack_depth`. Both are off by default; Unity has no equivalent.
- **Localisation** -- Unity has multiple line provider backends (built-in, Unity Localization package, Addressables). This implementation uses Godot's `TranslationServer` directly, with the text, asset and fallback locales set on the line provider.

## License

This project uses the Yarn Spinner Public License. You're free to use it in your own projects, commercial or otherwise. The only restrictions are around redistributing it as part of a competing dialogue tool, and using it to train AI models. Full details are in [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md). For a plain-language summary of the license terms and the intent behind its use, see the [YSPL FAQ](https://yarnspinner.dev/yspl).

## Installation

The addon is the `addons/yarn_spinner/` folder inside this repository. That folder is the only part that goes into your project; the rest of the repository (tests, compiler sources, this file) stays behind.

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Copy `addons/yarn_spinner/` into your Godot project's `addons/` directory, or symlink it from your checkout. The result should be `res://addons/yarn_spinner/plugin.cfg` in your project.
3. In the Godot editor, go to **Project > Project Settings > Plugins** and enable **Yarn Spinner**.
4. Drop your `.yarnproject` and `.yarn` files into your Godot project. The plugin compiles them automatically on import using its bundled compiler -- any time a `.yarn` file or the `.yarnproject` changes, Godot reimports and recompiles. No separate install is needed.
5. Only if the bundled compiler isn't available for your platform: install `ysc` (the [Yarn Spinner Console](https://github.com/YarnSpinnerTool/YarnSpinner-Console) tool) as a fallback with `dotnet tool install YarnSpinner.Console --global --version 3.2.2`.
6. Assign the imported `.yarnproject` to a Dialogue Runner in your scene.

If Godot reports missing dependencies on `res://addons/yarn_spinner/...` paths, or scripts fail to parse with `Could not find type "YarnDialogueRunner"`, the addon isn't at the path the project expects. The usual cause is copying the whole repository into `addons/`, which puts the addon at `addons/YarnSpinner-Godot-GDScript/addons/yarn_spinner`. Move the inner `yarn_spinner` folder so it sits directly under `addons/`, then reload the project.

## How It Works

The Yarn Spinner compiler (bundled with the addon, or `ysc`) compiles `.yarn` scripts into a binary protobuf program. This plugin reads that binary at import time, parses it into an in-memory program representation, and executes it in a stack-based virtual machine. The VM handles control flow, variable storage, function calls, and content delivery. A dialogue runner orchestrates the VM and routes lines, options, and commands to presenter nodes in your scene tree.

You write dialogue in Yarn, and the plugin compiles and runs it. Compilation happens automatically when Godot imports the `.yarnproject` file, using the compiler binary bundled with the addon (or `ysc` from your PATH as a fallback).

## Architecture

The plugin has three layers:

**Core** (`addons/yarn_spinner/core/`) contains the rntime engine. The protobuf parser reads compiled `.yarnproject` binaries. The virtual machine executes instructions. The yarn library provides built-in functions and operators. Variable storage holds game state. The line provider resolves localised text and applies markup. The saliency system selects content when multiple candidates match

**Dialogue Runner** (`addons/yarn_spinner/dialogue_runner.gd`) is the main node you add to your scene. It owns the VM, discovers commands from your scene tree, coordinates presenters, and exposes signals for dialogue lifecycle events. All configuration is done through its exported properties in the inspector.

**Presenters** (`addons/yarn_spinner/ui/`) display content to the player. The line presenter shows dialogue text with typewriter effects. The options presenter shows choice buttons. The voice over presenter plays audio files synced to lines. You can subclass `YarnDialoguePresenter` to build your own.

## Components

### YarnDialogueRunner

The central node. Add it to your scene, assign a `.yarnproject`, an call `start_dialogue()`. Key properties:

- `yarn_project` -- the compiled Yarn project to run
- `start_node` -- which node to begin from (default: `"Start"`)
- `auto_start` -- start dialogue when the scene loads
- `variable_storage` -- where game state is stored (auto-created if not set)
- `saliency_strategy` -- how to pick between competing content candidates
- `show_selected_option_as_line` -- re-display the chosen option as a line of dialogue
- `auto_discover_commands` -- find `_yarn_command_*` methods in your scene automatically

Signals: `dialogue_started`, `dialogue_completed`, `dialogue_cancelled`, `node_started`, `node_completed`, `command_unhandled`, `command_received`.

To choose a Yarn node from a dropdown on your own scripts, export a `String` with the `yarn_node` hint, naming the property that holds the Dialogue Runner or Yarn Project:

```gdscript
@export var dialogue_runner: YarnDialogueRunner
@export_custom(PROPERTY_HINT_NONE, "yarn_node:dialogue_runner") var start_at: String
```

### YarnLinePresenter

Displays a line of dialogue with optional typewriter animation (letter-by-letter or word-by-word). Expects a `RichTextLabel` for text and an optional `Label` for character names. Shows a continue indicator when the line is fully revealed.

### YarnOptionsPresenter

Shows dialogue choices as buttons. Creates a button per option, handles keyboard and mouse selection, and can hide or disable unavailable options.

### YarnDialoguePresenter

Base class for custom presenters. Override `run_line()` to handle lines and `run_options()` to handle choices. Multiple presenters can be active at once -- the runner coordinates them.

### YarnVariableStorage

Base class for game state storage. The built-in `YarnInMemoryVariableStorage` stores variables in a dictionary. Subclass it to save to disk or sync with your game systems. Supports typed access (`get_float`, `get_bool`, `get_string`) and change subscriptions with automatic cleanup.

### Custom Commands

Define commands in your scripts by naming methods `_yarn_command_<name>`. The runner discovers them automatically. Return a `Signal` to make the runner wait for it before continuing.
